lesson.title: Bearing Witness, Arriving Late: America and the Holocaust
lesson.summary: As Nazi Germany carried out the systematic genocide of six million Jews and millions of others, the U.S. government's response was slow and limited, shaped by restrictive immigration policy and bureaucratic indifference until late in the war.
lesson.body:
Adolf Hitler's Nazi regime built its ideology around a virulent antisemitism from its earliest years in power, steadily stripping German Jews of rights, property, and safety well before the war began. Once World War II started and Germany conquered much of Europe, that persecution escalated into industrialized mass murder. Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered approximately six million Jewish men, women, and children in what came to be called the Holocaust, along with millions of other victims targeted for persecution and death, including Roma people, people with disabilities, political prisoners, Soviet prisoners of war, and others the regime deemed undesirable. The killing took place through mass shootings, forced labor and starvation, and purpose-built death camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka, where victims were murdered in gas chambers on an industrial scale.

The American response to this unfolding catastrophe was, by the honest judgment of history, slow and inadequate. Strict immigration quotas dating back to the 1920s sharply limited how many refugees could legally enter the United States, and those quotas were not meaningfully expanded even as Nazi persecution intensified through the 1930s. In 1939, the ship St. Louis carried hundreds of Jewish refugees fleeing Germany toward Cuba and the United States, but both countries denied most passengers entry, forcing the ship back to Europe, where a substantial number of its passengers were later killed in the Holocaust. Within the U.S. State Department, officials responsible for processing visas, including Assistant Secretary of State Breckinridge Long, actively slowed and obstructed the granting of visas to Jewish refugees, keeping legal immigration far below even the limited quotas allowed.

It was not until January 1944, after Treasury Department officials uncovered and documented the State Department's obstruction and presented evidence of it directly to Roosevelt, that the president created the War Refugee Board to coordinate efforts to rescue European Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution. The board helped save thousands of lives in its final year and a half of operation, but it came very late, after years in which the killing had already claimed millions of victims. Allied military leaders also declined repeated requests to bomb rail lines leading to Auschwitz or the camp itself, a decision historians still debate, weighing military priorities and feasibility against the moral weight of the requests.

As Allied armies advanced into Germany in the final months of the war, American and other Allied troops liberated concentration camps including Buchenwald and Dachau in April 1945, and soldiers who entered these camps brought back firsthand, undeniable evidence of the scale of Nazi atrocities. The full scope of the Holocaust became clear to the American public largely only at the war's end, a sobering reminder of how much suffering had already occurred while the world's response remained limited and, for years, largely absent.
